children: The steelmaker is deploying AI-enabled surveillance, connected workforce systems and Integrated Remote Operation Centres to identify hazards and reduce workers’ exposure to high-risk environments

Tata Steel is scaling up artificial intelligence, connected workforce systems and remote operations to make industrial safety more predictive, with more than 10,000 CCTV cameras and AI-enabled surveillance deployed across its operations to identify unsafe behaviour and enable timely intervention.

Tatae past 15 years, Tata Steel has reduced its group-wide lost time injury frequency rate (LTIFR) by 38 per cent. The company is now using AI-enabled surveillance to detect unsafe acts and generate immediate alerts for supervisors, reducing dependence on manual monitoring of thousands of camera feeds.
Connected Workforce Systems
Tata Steel is deploying its Connected Workforce platform across India, using AI-enabled gate passes and beacons installed inside plants to track personnel movement and flag deviations.
The system is designed to help ensure workers enter only authorised and safe areas while enabling closer monitoring of movement across industrial facilities.
The company is also expanding Integrated Remote Operation Centres (iRoCs), enabling hazardous operations in mines and plants to be monitored and, where feasible, controlled remotely.

The centres bring together CCTV feeds, plant and machinery data and other critical information on large screens, helping reduce workers’ exposure to hazardous environments and improve coordination during emergencies.
Remote operations could also help attract younger workers to the steel industry by reducing exposure to hot, humid and high-noise workplaces.
AI Extends To Logistics
Tata Steel is also deploying digital safety systems across logistics operations. Around 8,000-10,000 trucks and trailers carrying raw materials or goods enter its plants every day.

Driver-fatigue monitoring systems use cameras to detect head movement and mobile-phone use, triggering alerts and automated warnings. Technology is also being used to prevent trucks from coming into contact with overhead cables.

The company’s digital safety systems include real-time hazard detection, Internet of Things (IoT) monitoring, predictive asset-health analysis, drones, smart surveillance and generative AI-enabled safety observation systems.
Tata Steel expects AI-powered hazard prediction, computer vision, digital twins, autonomous inspections, wearables and connected-worker technologies to become central to industrial safety by 2035.
Safety As Leadership Priority

Tata Steel’s safety performance is reviewed through its board-level Safety, Health & Environment Committee, Risk Management Committee and other leadership forums, with safety risks integrated into enterprise risk management.
The company’s Zero Harm philosophy applies equally to contract workers, who undergo mandatory induction, competency assessments, role-specific training, audits and performance monitoring.
Tata Steel has invested in two safety leadership development centres and benchmarks its practices against global steelmakers and other industries.

Its safety agenda also extends to mental health, heat stress, fatigue and ergonomics through a five-pillar wellness framework covering physical, emotional, occupational, social and financial wellbeing.
Decarbonisation And Capacity

Alongside its safety initiatives, Tata Steel remains committed to achieving Net Zero emissions by 2045 and is pursuing electric arc furnaces, renewable energy, biochar, HIsarna, EASyMelt and green-hydrogen technologies.The company has conducted a large-scale hydrogen injection trial in a blast furnace and found the technology technically feasible, although commercial deployment remains constrained by cost and availability.

Hydrogen prices would need to fall to around USD 1.5-2 per kg from roughly USD 4-6 per kg currently for large-scale steelmaking applications to become viable.Tata Steel estimates that its existing Indian sites have land to support capacity of up to 40 million tonnes. Future investments are expected to focus increasingly on specialised products, including electrical steel, heavy plates for shipbuilding and high-end steel for pipelines, including hydrogen transportation.

The company spent Rs 802.17 crore on environment, safety and compliance projects in FY2025-26, compared with Rs 1,036.25 crore in FY2024-25.Tata Steel reported a 19 per cent year-on-year rise in consolidated net profit to Rs 2,385.24 crore in the June quarter, while total income rose to Rs 61,026.97 crore in Q1 FY27 from Rs 53,466.79 crore in the corresponding quarter a year earlier.
